# General Instructions for Problem Sets

The goal of the problem sets is to give you practice thinking about and working with the concepts that we are covering. You may work together to complete these assignments. 

<b>Before completing a problem set, you should review the content videos for the week and it may be helpful to complete those before the related class periods as well.</b>

Use the link at the top of this webpage to turn in your completed assignment.

## Problem Set Specifications

To earn an "S":

* Completeness: Every question is thoroughly attempted.
* Accuracy: At least 80% of responses demonstrate correct logical reasoning, accurate quantitative calculations, and correct use of biological terms.
* Integrity & Sources: Citations are included where required, and work adheres to the Honor Code.

# Questions

1. Refer to one or more of the following readings from Gathering Moss to answer the questions below. Gathering Moss readings are: [In the Forest of the Waterbear](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1oeA1Argnoo3pJWv_I5jE_zGikq9knzjB/view?usp=sharing); [Choices](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1U17gcdmEqh09wX7uAFWLB8CMQVS2rH6n/view?usp=sharing); [Portrait of Splachnum](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1xgE9ohzUzKGSsSf0JjJqXgsGf6pX288C/view?usp=sharing).
    a. Provide 3 examples of non-competitive interspecific interactions that are described in the moss readings. Identify the type of interaction (e.g., commensalism? predation? parasitism?) and which organisms play which roles in the interaction.
    b. How would you describe the niche of a moss? Does it vary for different species of mosses?
    c. In these readings from Gathering Moss, identify at least 1 connection to other topics we’ve covered this semester.
    
2. As described in the content video on Competition, in Gauss’ experiments with competition in *Paramecium*, the same species always drove the other to extinction. Why is this consistent result expected from competition theory?

3. We think of invasive species as a human-facilitated phenomenon (and in many cases that’s totally accurate), but range expansion is also a natural phenomenon. After all, the species that are considered native in this part of Ohio could not have lived here 13,000 years ago when this place was covered with a mile of ice—they must have moved here from elsewhere, without human intervention. <b>Given this, what do you think happens in a community when a new species is introduced? Discuss what types of species interactions might occur and how that might influence the ability of the introduced species to persist in the new area.</b> (You may wish to focus on a particular example to help you illustrate these points.)

4. The Intermediate Disturbance Hypothesis (IDH) posits that the highest biodiversity will occur when an ecosystem experiences and intermediate level of disturbance; extremely low or extremely high disturbance is predicted to result in reduced diversity. In addition, ecologists generally believe that a more species-rich community is likely to be more resilient to disturbance than a species-poor community.
    a. Why would an intermediate level of disturbance support the highest species diversity? Relate to topics we have discussed previously. 
    b. What is meant by a community being “resilient” to disturbance? How could we measure this?
    c. Why might a diverse community be more resilient than a species-poor community?
    
5. As mentioned in the content video on succession, Clements viewed ecosystems “as analogous to an entire complex organism that, in the event of a disturbance, would pass through a series of stages to return to its climax comunity.” Why is this view inaccurate -- what’s wrong with it? What would be a more accurate way to describe our current understanding of the causes and process of ecological succession?

6. Read either [Binding up the Wounds: Mosses in Ecological Succession](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1VaaAViI3eMgr0T-j2ylysQJdYREQdHNd/view?usp=sharing) or  [Kickapoo](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1pJ5-Bf2UC0Q2bQoufOJ1P9W0ydAQpuCC/view?usp=sharing) How does the reading connect to what we’ve been covering in class? Give an example of how this reading relates to each of the following: 
    * competition 
    * community diversity and structure 
    * ecological succession

7. Do some searching through the readings or on the web to find an example of a trophic cascade. Describe a specific example of a trophic cascade; identify the primary organisms involved in the food web as well as their trophic positions in the web. Be sure to relate the effects of the trophic cascade to the flow of energy in the ecosystem.

8. Weekly Reflection. Consider this week’s material and reply to one or more of the following prompts:
    * What was confusing or interesting to you about this week’s material?
    * Did you have any key insights while studying this material?
    * Does anything from this week’s material particularly stick with you?
